mainTopic: The snake's seven-year pregnancy, and the story of רבי יהושע בן חנניה defeating the scholars of Athens
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining why a snake carries its young for seven years, based on the order of the words in its curse in בראשית. It asks why we should not use the goat-to-cat ratio, which would give only fifteen months, and gives two answers: the word "all" in the פסוק, and the rule that a curse is read at its harshest. Then comes a story. The קיסר asks רבי יהושע בן חנניה how long a snake carries its young. He answers seven years and defends this against the Athens scholars' experiment. When he claims the Jewish חכמים are wiser, the emperor sends him to defeat the sixty Athens scholars and bring them back. רבי יהושע outwits a butcher and the guards, greets the scholars wisely, and wins a long contest of riddles, often by turning their impossible questions back on them. In the end he brings them onto his ship, sets sail, and takes some of their native soil with him. The story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The order of the words in the verse decides the comparison
steps.stepSummary: The verse lists בהמה before חיה. So the snake is compared to the בהמה (donkey), which was cursed compared to the חיה (cat).
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the verse say "from all the wild beasts and from all the domesticated animals"? No, it says "from all the domesticated animals and from all the wild beasts"! That means the snake is cursed more than the domesticated animal, and the domesticated animal was already cursed more than the wild animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a challenge on the previous amud: maybe the snake should only be compared to the cat. The answer comes from the order of the words in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because בהמה comes first, the curse works as a chain: חיה, then בהמה, then snake. A donkey (12 months) is cursed about 7 times more than a cat (52 days). So the snake is cursed about 7 times more than the donkey, which is about seven years.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written...? (a way of saying the verse does not say that)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'cursed' means a longer pregnancy. The longer an animal carries its young, the more 'cursed' it is considered.

phrases.english: Is it written:
"From all the wild beasts and from all the domesticated animals"?
phrases.notes: This is the order the challenger needed. The real פסוק says it the other way around.

phrases.english: It is written: "From all the domesticated animals and from all the wild beasts"!
phrases.notes: This is the snake's curse in בראשית, chapter 3.

phrases.english: It (the snake) is cursed more than the domesticated animal,
which was itself cursed more than the wild animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge earlier, which suggested comparing the snake to the cat.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of the word order in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The snake is compared to the חיה, which would give a short pregnancy.
steps.terutzMaskana: The snake is compared to the בהמה, which was cursed compared to the חיה, so the snake carries for seven years.

steps.title: Why not use the goat-to-cat ratio of one to three?
steps.stepSummary: Maybe the ratio should come from the goat (5 months) compared to the cat (52 days), about 1 to 3. That would make the snake's pregnancy 15 months.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: just as domesticated animals were cursed more than wild animals at a ratio of one to three (which case is that? a goat compared to a cat), so too the snake was cursed more than the domesticated animal at one to three, which comes to fifteen months!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the number seven. Why pick the donkey, when the goat gives a smaller ratio?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chain idea is accepted, but which בהמה should we use? A goat carries 5 months, about 3 times a cat's 52 days. Three times the goat's 5 months gives the snake only 15 months.

phrases.english: But say: just as was cursed
the domesticated animal more than the wild animal, by one to three,
and which case is that? A goat compared to a cat,
phrases.notes: A goat carries about 5 months and a cat about 52 days, so roughly three times as long.

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ נִתְקַלֵּל הוּא מִבְּהֵמָה אֶחָד לְשָׁלֹשׁ,
phrases.english: so too it (the snake) was cursed more than the domesticated animal by one to three,
which comes to fifteen months!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the chain from step 1 but challenges which בהמה should set the ratio.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that the snake carries for seven years, based on the donkey
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Other domesticated animals, like the goat, give a smaller ratio. Why choose the donkey and get the harsher number?

steps.title: The verse says all the animals, including the most cursed
steps.stepSummary: "מכל הבהמה" means the snake is cursed more than every domesticated animal, even the most cursed one, the donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: it is written "from all the domesticated animals."
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first answer to the goat challenge. The word "all" in the פסוק settles it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the snake is cursed more than all the domesticated animals, we must measure it against the most cursed one, the donkey. The goat is not enough, so the ratio of 1 to 7 stays.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces one of several answers)

phrases.english: If you want, say:
It is written "from ALL the domesticated animals."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the goat challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the word 'all' in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any domesticated animal, like the goat, could set the ratio.
steps.terutzMaskana: The most cursed domesticated animal, the donkey, sets the ratio, so the answer stays seven years.

steps.title: A curse is given in its harshest form
steps.stepSummary: Since this is a curse, we read it in the most severe way the verse allows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say: it is a curse, so the verse puts the heaviest curse on it.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second, separate answer to the goat challenge. It is based on the nature of a curse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the פסוק can be read in two ways and the subject is a punishment, we choose the harsher reading. So the donkey ratio (seven years) wins over the goat ratio (fifteen months).

keyTerms.meaning: Throw upon it, impose on it

steps.whatToRemember: The snake carries for seven years. It is cursed more than the donkey just as the donkey is cursed more than the cat, either because of the word "all" or because a curse is read at its harshest.

phrases.english: Or if you want, say: it is a curse,
so throw the full curse upon it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same challenge as step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical reasoning: a curse gets its most severe reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Choose the milder ratio of 1 to 3.
steps.terutzMaskana: Choose the harsher ratio of 1 to 7, which gives seven years.

steps.title: The emperor asks how long a snake carries its young
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר asks רבי יהושע בן חנניה how long a snake's pregnancy lasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: After how long a pregnancy does a snake give birth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about the same topic, the snake's pregnancy. This question sets up the debate that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story tests the seven-year rule we just learned against the claims of the Greek scholars.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה:
phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya:
A snake, after how long a pregnancy does it give birth?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story on the same subject as steps 1 to 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long a snake's pregnancy lasts

steps.title: רבי יהושע answers: seven years
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן חנניה answers that a snake carries for seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives the same answer we learned from the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His answer matches the seven years worked out above from the snake's curse.

phrases.english: He said to him: After seven years.

steps.title: The Athens experiment showed three years
steps.stepSummary: The emperor objects: the scholars of Athens mated snakes and they gave birth after three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the elders of Athens mated them, and they gave birth after three years!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor challenges the seven-year answer with what was seen in an experiment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If snakes were seen giving birth three years after mating, then seven years seems wrong.

phrases.english: But the elders of Athens mated them (the snakes),
and they gave birth after three (years)!

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: What was actually seen (birth three years after mating) contradicts seven years.

steps.title: Those snakes were already pregnant for four years
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that the snakes were already four years into their pregnancy before the experiment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those snakes had already been pregnant from before for four years.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע explains away the experiment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four years before the experiment plus the three years seen during it adds up to seven years. So the experiment does not disprove the rule.

phrases.english: Those were already pregnant from before for four (years).

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the facts of the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The pregnancy began when they were mated.
steps.terutzMaskana: The pregnancy began four years earlier, so the total is seven.

steps.title: But they mated, so they could not already be pregnant
steps.stepSummary: The emperor objects: the snakes mated, and animals mate only when they are not yet pregnant.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they were mating!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor challenges רבי יהושע's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor assumes animals mate only in order to become pregnant. So an animal that mates must not have been pregnant before.

phrases.english: But they were actually mating!

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the snakes were already pregnant
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Animals do not mate while pregnant, so the snakes could not have been pregnant before.

steps.title: Snakes mate like people do
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that snakes, like people, mate even when the female is already pregnant.
steps.simpleTranslation: They too mate like a person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the emperor's challenge about mating, which ends the argument over the snakes themselves. The story goes on in the next step, where the emperor questions the Athens scholars' wisdom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike most animals, snakes do not mate only to reproduce. So mating does not prove they were not already pregnant, and the seven-year answer stands.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהושע defends the seven-year pregnancy: the Athens snakes were already four years pregnant, and snakes mate even while pregnant, like people.

phrases.english: They too mate like a person.
phrases.notes: He means people mate not only to have children, and snakes are the same.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: Animals mate only when not pregnant.
steps.terutzMaskana: Snakes mate even when pregnant, so the seven-year rule stands.

steps.title: The emperor: aren't the Athens scholars wise?
steps.stepSummary: The emperor pushes back on רבי יהושע's answer by pointing to the wisdom of the Athens scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: But aren't they wise men?
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor is not raising a new fact. He is asking how רבי יהושע dares to disagree with such famous wise men.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 6–10, רבי יהושע explained away every result from the Athens experiment. Now the emperor attacks the person behind the answer. If the Athens scholars are so wise, maybe their conclusion is simply right.

phrases.english: But aren't they wise men?
phrases.notes: "They" means the scholars of Athens from the experiment in step 7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהושע's right to reject the Athens findings
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's dismissal of the Athens experiment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Experts this wise should be trusted over him.

steps.title: We are wiser than they are
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that the Jewish חכמים are wiser than the Athens scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are wiser than them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the emperor's challenge in a few bold words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny that the Athens scholars are wise. He says the Jewish חכמים are wiser, so his answer stands. This claim sets up the rest of the story, where he has to prove it.

phrases.english: We are wiser than they.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the premise that their wisdom settles the matter
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Athens scholars' wisdom makes them right
steps.terutzMaskana: The Jewish חכמים are wiser, so their view wins

steps.title: The emperor's dare: beat them and bring them
steps.stepSummary: The emperor challenges רבי יהושע to prove his claim by defeating the Athens scholars and bringing them to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you are wiser, go defeat them and bring them to me!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor turns רבי יהושע's claim into a mission. This sets up the whole journey that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying "we are wiser" is easy, so the emperor asks for proof. רבי יהושע must win against them and bring them back as captives.

phrases.aramaic: אִי חֲכִימַתְּ, זִיל זַכִּינְהוּ וְאַיְתִינְהוּ לִי!
phrases.english: If you are wiser, go defeat them and bring them to me!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי חֲכִימַתְּ, זִיל זַכִּינְהוּ וְאַיְתִינְהוּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבי יהושע's claim into a test
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע must prove his claim by defeating the Athens scholars

steps.title: How many scholars are there?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks how many Athens scholars there are.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: How many are there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע accepts the mission and asks a practical question to get ready.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He needs the number to plan how to bring them all back. The answer will decide the size of the ship he asks for.

phrases.english: He said to him: How many are there?
phrases.notes: Here רבי יהושע is asking the emperor.

steps.title: Sixty men
steps.stepSummary: The emperor answers that there are sixty scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sixty men.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor answers the question: there are sixty scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This number matters right away. The ship רבי יהושע requests is built around sixty, one room for each scholar.

phrases.english: Sixty men.

steps.title: A ship with sixty rooms
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע asks for a ship with sixty rooms, each holding sixty mattresses, and the emperor builds it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Make me a ship with sixty rooms, and in each room sixty mattresses. The emperor made it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע prepares a ship to carry the sixty scholars home, and the emperor has it built.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sixty rooms match the sixty scholars. This shows how confident רבי יהושע is that he will win and bring them all back. The reason for the sixty mattresses in each room comes out in step 60.

phrases.english: He said to him: Make me a ship
that has sixty rooms in it,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל בֵּיתָא אִית בַּהּ שִׁיתִּין בִּיסְתַּרְקֵי.
phrases.english: and each room has sixty mattresses in it.
He made it for him.
phrases.notes: The emperor had it built.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבֵיד לִי סְפִינְתָּא דְּאִית בַּהּ שִׁיתִּין בָּתֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the number sixty to plan the ship
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ship is built to hold all sixty scholars

steps.title: Buying the butcher's head
steps.stepSummary: In Athens, רבי יהושע asks a butcher if his head is for sale, agrees on half a זוז, and pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he got there, to a butcher shop, he found a man skinning an animal. He asked: Is your head for sale? The man said: Yes. For how much? For half a זוז. He paid him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע sets a clever word trap for a butcher. He asks about "your head," and the butcher assumes he means the animal's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "your head" can mean the butcher's own head or the head of the animal he is selling. The butcher agrees to a price and takes the money, not realizing what he just agreed to. The trap will close in the next step.

phrases.english: When he arrived there, at a butcher shop,
phrases.notes: "There" means Athens. He sailed there on the ship.

phrases.english: he found a certain man
who was skinning an animal.
He said to him: Is your head for sale?
phrases.notes: The wording is tricky on purpose. It can mean the butcher's own head.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.
He said to him: For how much?
He said to him: For half a zuz.
He gave it to him.
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע paid the money.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The butcher agrees to sell "your head" for half a זוז

steps.title: The trap: show me the entrance
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע claims he bought the butcher's own head, then offers to let him off if he shows the entrance to the scholars' meeting place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Afterward he said: Did I say the animal's head? If you want me to let you go, go show me the entrance to the house of Athens.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע springs the trap and uses it to get what he really wants: the hidden entrance to where the scholars meet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He insists he paid for the butcher's own head, not the animal's. He never truly wants it. It is his leverage, and he will drop the claim in exchange for directions.

phrases.english: In the end, he said to him:
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע is the speaker here.

phrases.english: Did I say to you the head of the animal?
phrases.notes: He means: I bought your head, so now it is mine.

phrases.english: He said to him: If you want me to let you go,
go show me
the entrance of the house of Athens.
phrases.notes: He means the meeting place of the Athens scholars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the trap set in the purchase
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The butcher will be released if he reveals the entrance

steps.title: The butcher is afraid
steps.stepSummary: The butcher objects that anyone who reveals the entrance is killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I'm afraid, because anyone who shows it gets killed.
steps.whatsHappening: The butcher raises a problem with the deal: showing the entrance would cost him his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how secret and well-protected the Athens scholars were. רבי יהושע now has to find a way around the danger.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am afraid,
because anyone who shows it, they kill him.

steps.kashyaTarget: The demand to show the entrance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Showing it openly would get the butcher killed.

steps.title: Mark it with a bundle of reeds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells the butcher to carry reeds and stand them up at the entrance, as if he were resting.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Carry a bundle of reeds, and when you get there, stand it up like someone taking a rest.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע solves the butcher's fear with a secret signal, so the butcher never has to point openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The butcher just looks like a worker putting down his load to rest. Nobody can say he "showed" anyone, yet רבי יהושע learns exactly where the entrance is.

phrases.english: He said to him: Carry a bundle of reeds,
and when you arrive there,
phrases.notes: "There" means the entrance.

phrases.english: stand it up like one who is resting.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: Revealing the entrance means openly pointing it out
steps.terutzMaskana: A hidden signal reveals it without any open pointing

steps.title: Guards inside and outside
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע finds guards inside and outside the entrance, who are killed if footprints show anyone entering or leaving.
steps.simpleTranslation: He found guards inside and guards outside. If they saw footprints going in, they killed the outside guards; if going out, they killed the inside guards.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that he has found the entrance, רבי יהושע discovers how tightly it is guarded. This sets up his next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The outside guards are blamed if anyone gets in, and the inside guards are blamed if anyone gets out. So entering or leaving seems impossible, and רבי יהושע will need a new trick.

phrases.english: He found guards on the inside
and guards on the outside,
for if they saw a footprint going in,
they would kill the outer ones,
and if going out, they would kill the inner ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the next obstacle after finding the entrance
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The entrance is guarded so that no one can enter or leave without the guards being punished

steps.title: The sandal trick gets rid of the guards
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע turns his sandal backwards twice. This leads the authorities to kill first the inner guards and then all the guards.
steps.simpleTranslation: He turned his sandal around, and they killed the inner guards. He turned his sandal around again, and they killed all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע uses the footprint rule from the previous step against the guards. Fake footprints get the guards blamed and killed, so the entrance is left open for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guards were killed if footprints showed that someone went in or came out. First he made prints that looked like someone had left, so the inner guards were blamed. Then he reversed the sandal again to make prints that looked like someone had entered, so all the guards were blamed, and nobody was left to stop him.

keyTerms.meaning: He turned it over or reversed it

phrases.english: He reversed his sandal —
phrases.notes: He turned it backwards, so his footprints pointed the opposite way from where he was really walking.

phrases.english: they killed the inner guards;
he reversed his sandal again —
they killed all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the guard problem described in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע removes both sets of guards by faking footprints.

steps.title: The problem of whom to greet first
steps.stepSummary: Inside, the young sages sit above and the elders sit below. רבי יהושע worries that greeting the young ones first will anger the elders.
steps.simpleTranslation: He found young men sitting above and old men sitting below. He said to himself: If I greet these first, those will kill me. They think: We are more important, because we are older, and they are just children.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע walks into the room and runs into a new problem about respect. The גמרא is setting up how he will solve it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you greet whoever sits in the higher, more honored place first, and here that is the young sages. But the elders believe that age should come first, so greeting the young ones first would insult the elders and put his life in danger. Either choice offends one group.

phrases.english: He found young men sitting above,
and old men sitting below.
He said: If I greet these first,
phrases.notes: "These" means the young men sitting above.

phrases.english: those will kill me,
phrases.notes: "Those" means the elders sitting below.

phrases.english: because they think: We are more important,
since we are much older,
phrases.notes: Literally "we are harder," which here means older and more seasoned.

phrases.english: and they are just children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Once he is inside, a new obstacle comes up.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Greeting either group first would offend the other group.

steps.title: A greeting to everyone at once
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says "Greetings to you" to the whole room, without singling out either group.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Peace to you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע solves the greeting problem by greeting the whole room together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the greeting goes to everyone at the same moment, neither group was greeted first. Nobody can feel insulted, and he stays safe.

phrases.english: He said: Peace to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the problem raised in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general greeting avoids honoring one group over the other.

steps.title: The sages ask why he has come
steps.stepSummary: The sages of Athens ask רבי יהושע what he is doing there.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What is your business here?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages question the stranger who just walked in. This sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No outsider was supposed to be able to get in, so they want to know who he is and what he wants.

keyTerms.meaning: Your business, what you are doing

phrases.english: They said to him: What is your business here?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The sages respond to his greeting.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who he is and why he came.

steps.title: He says he has come to learn wisdom
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says he is a Jewish sage who wants to learn wisdom from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I am a wise man of the Jews, and I want to learn wisdom from you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers their question in a humble, flattering way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He presents himself as a student who has come to learn, not as an enemy. This gives them a reason to talk with him instead of killing him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אֲנָא חַכִּימָא דִיהוּדָאֵי אֲנָא,
phrases.english: He said to them: I am a wise man of the Jews,
and I want to learn wisdom from you.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is a Jewish sage who has come to learn wisdom.

steps.title: The stakes of the contest are set
steps.stepSummary: The sages say they will test him with questions. רבי יהושע agrees and sets the stakes: if they win they may do as they like with him, and if he wins they must eat with him on his ship.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: If so, we will ask you questions. He said to them: Fine. If you win, do whatever you want to me. And if I beat you, come eat with me on my ship.
steps.whatsHappening: The sages turn his visit into a test of wisdom, and both sides agree on what the winner gets. This sets up the riddles that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he says he is wise, they want to test him first. The stakes are high on both sides. Losing could cost him his life, while their "meal on the ship" sounds harmless now but becomes important later in the story.

phrases.english: They said: If so, we will ask you questions!
He said to them: Fine,

phrases.aramaic: אִי זָכֵיתוּ — כֹּל דְּבָעֵיתוּ עֲבִידוּ בִּי,
phrases.english: if you win, do whatever you want to me,
and if I beat you,
come eat with me on my ship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The sages respond to his claim that he is wise.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A contest of questions is set up, with stakes for each side.

steps.title: The first riddle: the rejected suitor
steps.stepSummary: The sages ask why a man who was turned down for marriage would go and propose to an even more important family.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: A man went and asked for a woman, and they did not give her to him. Why would he think to go to a family that is higher than the first?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages give רבי יהושע their first test question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The riddle seems to have no sensible answer. If a lower family turned him down, it looks foolish to try a higher one. They are testing whether he can explain behavior that seems to make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Who are higher or more distinguished

phrases.english: They said to him: A certain man who went
and asked for a woman, and they did not give her to him,
why would he think to go
to a place that is higher than the first?
phrases.notes: He means a family more important than the one that turned him down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the first question of the contest agreed on in step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What sense it makes for a rejected suitor to try a more important family.

steps.title: The peg answer: his match may be higher up
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע shows with a peg that it does not go in low on the wall but does go in higher. He explains that the man may find the wife meant for him in the higher family.
steps.simpleTranslation: He took a peg and pushed it into the lower part of the wall, and it did not go in. He pushed it into the higher part, and it went in. He said: This man too may find the woman meant for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the riddle with a demonstration you can see instead of only words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something that fails in a low place can still succeed in a higher place, if that is where it fits. In the same way, being turned down by one family says nothing about another. A match depends on who is meant for whom, not on status, so the higher family may hold his destined wife.

keyTerms.meaning: The woman meant for him (his destined match)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהושע wins the first riddle with a picture you can see. A rejection in one place does not mean failure in a higher place, because a match depends on who is meant for whom.

phrases.english: He took a peg,
pushed it into the lower part of the wall, and it did not go in,
then into the upper part, and it went in.
phrases.notes: Higher up, there was a spot where the peg fit.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: הַאי נָמֵי מִיתְרְמֵי בַּת מַזָּלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He said: This man too may happen upon the woman meant for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the riddle asked in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The man may find his destined match in the higher family, just as the peg fit in the higher spot on the wall.

steps.title: Why does a lender who lost money keep lending?
steps.stepSummary: The sages of Athens ask why a lender who had to seize a borrower's property would lend again.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man lent money and had to collect by seizing property. Why would he lend again?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages of Athens ask רבי יהושע a new riddle. A lender already had trouble once, so why would he risk lending again?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is built just like the marriage question in Step 28. Someone had a bad experience, yet he tries again. They want רבי יהושע to explain behavior that seems illogical.

keyTerms.meaning: Seizes or repossesses property to collect a debt
What did he see? (Why would he?)

phrases.english: A man who lends and repossesses,
why would he see fit to lend again?

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבְרָא דְּאוֹזֵיף וְטָרֵיף, מַאי חֲזָא דַּהֲדַר אוֹזֵיף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new riddle in the same contest
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a lender who was burned once keeps lending

steps.title: The parable of the bundle of reeds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers with a parable: a man keeps cutting reeds onto a bundle he can't lift, until someone comes along to help him lift it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man goes to the marsh and cuts a bundle of reeds but can't lift it. He keeps cutting and piling more on top, until someone happens by and helps him lift it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers with a story from daily life. People don't give up just because the first try didn't work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man doesn't quit cutting just because he can't lift the load alone. He trusts that a helper will eventually come. The lender is the same: he keeps lending because sooner or later he will find a good borrower.

keyTerms.meaning: A marsh or pond where reeds grow

phrases.english: He said to them:
A man goes to the marsh,

phrases.aramaic: קְטַל קַמָּא טוּנָא וְלָא מָצֵי בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: first he cuts a bundle but cannot lift it,
so he cuts more and places it on top,
until a person happens by and lifts it for him.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the one in square brackets. Both mean 'happens to come.'

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבְרָא אֲזַל לְאַגְמָא, קְטַל קַמָּא טוּנָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: People keep trying, trusting that the right partner (helper or borrower) will eventually come

steps.title: Tell us some nonsense
steps.stepSummary: The sages of Athens challenge רבי יהושע to tell them a nonsense story.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Tell us some nonsense!
steps.whatsHappening: The sages give רבי יהושע a strange new challenge: make up something absurd. This sets up the story in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a request, not a real question looking for information. The test is whether he can make up something that is clearly impossible.

phrases.english: They said to him:
Tell us words of nonsense!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge in the contest

steps.title: The mule that gave birth with an IOU around its neck
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells of a mule that gave birth, and the baby had a note around its neck saying its father's family owed it 100,000 זוז.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a mule that gave birth. A note hung on the baby, and it said that its father's house owed it a hundred thousand זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע tells a wild story about a mule giving birth to a baby wearing an IOU.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mules can't have babies, so the story is impossible from the start. The detail about a debt from 'its father's house' is a playful way to make it even more absurd.

keyTerms.meaning: A female mule (mules cannot give birth)

phrases.english: He said to them:
There was a certain mule that gave birth,
and a note was hanging on it,
phrases.notes: The note was hanging on the newborn baby.

phrases.english: and written on it was

phrases.aramaic: דְּמַסֵּיק בְּבֵי אַבָּא מְאָה אַלְפָּא זוּזֵי.
phrases.english: that it is owed by its father's house a hundred thousand zuz.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A story of a mule giving birth

steps.title: But can a mule give birth?
steps.stepSummary: The sages object that a mule cannot give birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: But can a mule give birth?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages fall into the trap and complain that the story is impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By objecting, they treat the story as a real claim. That walks them right into the answer in the next step.

phrases.english: They said to him:
But does a mule give birth?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the story of Step 33
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mules are infertile, so the story can't be true

steps.title: That's exactly why it's nonsense
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע replies that this is exactly what makes it nonsense.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: These are words of nonsense.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע points out that their objection proves he did what they asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They asked for nonsense, and their own complaint shows the story is nonsense. He wins this round.
steps.whatToRemember: The mule round: the sages' own objection proves that רבי יהושע did exactly what they asked.

phrases.english: He said to them:
These are the words of nonsense.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets and some have the ones in square brackets. Both mean 'these are.'

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story fails because it's impossible
steps.terutzMaskana: Being impossible is exactly what makes it nonsense, as requested

steps.title: How do you salt salt that went bad?
steps.stepSummary: The sages ask what you use to preserve salt once it starts to spoil.
steps.simpleTranslation: When salt goes bad, what do you salt it with?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages ask a trick question. Salt is what preserves other foods, so what would preserve salt?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question quietly assumes something false: salt never spoils. The sages are trying to make רבי יהושע answer an impossible question.

phrases.english: Salt, when it spoils,
with what does one salt it?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְחָא כִּי סָרְיָא, בְּמַאי מָלְחִי לַהּ

steps.title: With a mule's placenta
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that you salt it with the placenta of a mule.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: With the placenta of a mule.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives an answer that is just as impossible as the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mule doesn't give birth, so it has no placenta. He answers an impossible question with an impossible answer.

phrases.english: He said to them:
With the placenta of a mule.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An impossible remedy: a mule's placenta

steps.title: Does a mule even have a placenta?
steps.stepSummary: The sages object that mules have no placenta.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there such a thing as a mule's placenta?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages again object that his answer is impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They attack his answer, but they don't notice that their own question had the same flaw.

phrases.english: But is there a placenta for a mule?
phrases.notes: These are the sages talking, even though the גמרא doesn't say 'they said.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the answer of Step 37
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mules don't give birth, so they have no placenta

steps.title: And does salt spoil?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע turns the question back on them: salt doesn't spoil either.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does salt spoil?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע shows that his impossible answer fits their impossible question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Salt never spoils, so the question had no real answer. An impossible question gets an impossible answer, and their trick falls apart.
steps.whatToRemember: The salt round: a question built on a false assumption is answered with an equally false answer.

phrases.english: And does salt spoil?
phrases.notes: Now רבי יהושע is talking, answering them back.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Exposing the false assumption of the original question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The answer is flawed because mules have no placenta
steps.terutzMaskana: The question was equally flawed, since salt doesn't spoil

steps.title: Build us a house in the air
steps.stepSummary: The sages demand that רבי יהושע build them a house in midair.
steps.simpleTranslation: Build us a house in the air of the world!
steps.whatsHappening: The sages give an impossible task. This sets up רבי יהושע's clever response.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a demand, not a request for information. They expect him to admit it can't be done.

phrases.english: Build us a house in the air of the world!

steps.title: He floats up and asks for building supplies
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says a Divine Name, hovers in the air, and asks them to bring up bricks and mortar.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said a Name and hung between sky and earth. He said to them: Bring me up bricks and mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע takes his position in the air and puts the burden back on them: bring up the materials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does his part by being up in the air, ready to build. Now they would have to bring bricks up to him, and they can't, so the impossible part is on their side.

phrases.english: He uttered a Name,
phrases.notes: A holy Name of ה׳, which let him rise into the air.

phrases.english: and hung between the sky and the earth.
He said to them:
Bring up to me bricks and mortar.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שֵׁם, תְּלָא בֵּין רְקִיעָא לְאַרְעָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is ready to build in the air if they supply the materials

steps.title: Where is the center of the world?
steps.stepSummary: The sages ask where the exact center of the world is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where is the middle of the world?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages ask a question that seems impossible to answer exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody could prove where the exact center is, so any answer seems open to attack.

phrases.english: The middle of the world, where is it?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The location of the world's center

steps.title: Right here
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע raises his finger and says: here.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised his finger and said to them: Here.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע confidently points to where he is and says this is the center.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He doesn't try to prove it. He just claims a spot, setting up the next exchange.

phrases.english: He raised his finger,
and said to them: Here.

steps.title: Who says so?
steps.stepSummary: The sages challenge him: how do you know?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: And who says so?
steps.whatsHappening: The sages challenge his claim and ask for proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They think they've caught him, since he can't prove the center is where he points.

phrases.english: They said to him: And who says?

steps.title: Bring ropes and measure
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells them to bring ropes and measure it themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bring ropes and measure.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע puts the burden of proof back on them: if you doubt me, go measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measuring the whole world is impossible, so they can never disprove him. The impossible task lands back on them, just like the bricks and mortar.
steps.whatToRemember: In these rounds רבי יהושע keeps turning impossible challenges back on the people who asked them.

phrases.english: Bring ropes and measure.
phrases.notes: These are רבי יהושע's words back to them.

steps.terutzMaskana: They are free to measure, which they can never do

steps.title: Bring a pit from the field into the city
steps.stepSummary: The elders give רבי יהושע an impossible task: move a pit from the field into the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a pit in the field. Bring it into the city!
steps.whatsHappening: The elders of אתונא set up a new trick challenge. They ask רבי יהושע to move a hole in the ground into town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit is not an object you can carry; it is just empty space in the ground. The demand is built to be impossible, so they can see whether he gets stuck.

phrases.english: We have a pit in the field,
bring it into the city!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the measuring answer, the elders start a new riddle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can he move an immovable pit into the city?

steps.title: Braid ropes of bran and I will bring it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers with an equally impossible condition: make me ropes out of bran.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Braid me ropes out of bran, and I will pull it in.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע doesn't argue. He says he'll do it, as long as they first give him an impossible tool.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ropes made of bran would fall apart at once. He matches one impossible demand with another, which shows that their request was nonsense.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Braid ropes of bran for me, and I will bring it in.
phrases.notes: Bran is the loose, crumbly husk of grain, so a rope made of it could never hold together.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An impossible request deserves an impossible condition: ropes of bran.

steps.title: Sew up a broken millstone
steps.stepSummary: The elders ask him to sew a broken stone mill back together.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a mill that broke. Sew it!
steps.whatsHappening: The elders give another impossible task: stitch together a cracked stone mill.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You sew cloth with thread. You cannot sew stone. The challenge again tests whether he will get flustered.

phrases.english: We have a mill that broke; sew it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new impossible task, same pattern as the pit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can a stone mill be sewn?

steps.title: Pull threads out of the mill and I will sew it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says: first pull threads out of the stone, and I'll sew with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Pull threads out of it for me, and I will sew it.
steps.whatsHappening: He again turns the impossible task back on them. Give me thread made from the stone itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sewing needs threads, so he asks them to supply threads from the millstone. Since they can't, they can't blame him for not sewing.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: כְּרוּכוּ לִי מִינַּיהּ גַּרְדֵי וְאִיחַיְּיטַיהּ.
phrases.english: He said: Pull threads out of it for me, and I will sew it.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Threads must come from the mill itself, which is impossible.

steps.title: How do you harvest a field of knives
steps.stepSummary: The elders ask what tool is used to harvest a field that grows knives.
steps.simpleTranslation: A field of knives, with what do they harvest it?
steps.whatsHappening: The elders ask a riddle about an imaginary field where knives grow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes a thing that doesn't exist. They want to see what he will say.

phrases.english: A field of knives, with what does one harvest it?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: What tool harvests a field of knives?

steps.title: With a donkey's horn
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers: with the horn of a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: With a donkey's horn.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives an answer that sounds strange on purpose. It sets up the next exchange.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Donkeys have no horns. He gives a made-up answer to match their made-up question.

phrases.english: With the horn of a donkey.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A tool that doesn't exist: a donkey's horn.

steps.title: But does a donkey have a horn
steps.stepSummary: The elders object: there's no such thing as a donkey's horn.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is there such a thing as a horn on a donkey?
steps.whatsHappening: The elders attack his answer, pointing out that donkeys don't have horns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They fell into his trap. By objecting that his answer is unreal, they set him up to point out that their question was unreal too.

phrases.english: But is there a horn on a donkey?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The tool he named doesn't exist.

steps.title: But is there a field of knives
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers back: and is there a field of knives?
steps.simpleTranslation: And is there such a thing as a field of knives?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע throws their own words back at them: their question was just as impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An imaginary question gets an imaginary answer. The same words, וּמִי אִיכָּא, show the two sides are equal.
steps.whatToRemember: This is רבי יהושע's whole method in this story: when given a nonsense question, he answers in a way that shows the question was nonsense.

phrases.english: And is there a field of knives?

steps.terutzResolutionType: Turning the challenge back on the questioner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His answer is invalid because donkeys have no horns.
steps.terutzMaskana: Their question was equally unreal, so an unreal answer fits.

steps.title: Which egg is from the black hen
steps.stepSummary: The elders bring two eggs and ask which came from a black hen and which from a white hen.
steps.simpleTranslation: They brought him two eggs and said to him: Which is from the black hen, and which is from the white hen?
steps.whatsHappening: The elders test him with a question that has no way to be answered just by looking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eggs from black and white hens look the same. They want him to admit he can't tell.

phrases.english: They brought him two eggs,
and said to him: Which is from the black hen,
and which is from the white hen?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can he tell which egg came from which colored hen?

steps.title: Which cheese is from the black goat
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע brings two cheeses and asks them which came from a black goat and which from a white goat.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought them two cheeses and said to them: Which is from the black goat, and which is from the white goat?
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of answering, רבי יהושע hands them the same kind of puzzle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cheese from a black or white goat also looks the same. By asking them a matching question, he shows their question can't be answered either.

phrases.english: He, in turn, brought them two cheeses,
and said to them: Which is from the black goat,
and which is from the white goat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the egg test with a matching puzzle.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A parallel question showing theirs has no answer.

steps.title: Where does a dead chick's spirit leave the egg
steps.stepSummary: The elders ask: when a chick dies inside a sealed egg, where does its life-spirit go out?
steps.simpleTranslation: A chick that died, from where does its spirit go out?
steps.whatsHappening: The elders ask a puzzle about a chick that dies inside a closed eggshell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shell has no opening, so they ask how the spirit could get out.

phrases.english: A chick that died,
phrases.notes: He means a chick that dies while still inside the sealed egg.

phrases.english: from where does its spirit exit?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: How does the spirit leave a closed egg?

steps.title: It leaves the way it came in
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers: it leaves from the same place it entered.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where it came in, it went out.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives a short answer: the spirit leaves the same way it got in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirit entered the closed egg without any opening, so it can leave the same way. Their 'problem' answers itself.

phrases.english: From where it entered, it went out.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The spirit exits the same way it entered.

steps.title: Show us an item not worth the damage it causes
steps.stepSummary: The elders ask him to show them an object whose value is less than the loss it causes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Show us a utensil that is not worth the damage it causes!
steps.whatsHappening: The elders ask him to prove, with a real example, that such an item exists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time they want him to show something real, not just answer with words. That sets up his demonstration in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: אַחְוִי לַן מָנָא דְּלָא שָׁוֵי חֲבִילֵיהּ!
phrases.english: Show us a utensil that is not worth the damage it causes!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחְוִי לַן מָנָא דְּלָא שָׁוֵי חֲבִילֵיהּ
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real example of an object worth less than the damage it causes.

steps.title: The big mat that forces you to break the gate
steps.stepSummary: Each elder brings a mat and spreads it out. It's too big for the gate, so the gate has to be broken. That is the item not worth its damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: He had each one bring a mat and spread it out. It would not fit through the gate. He said to them: Bring axes and break it down. This is a utensil not worth the damage it causes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers by actually doing it. A cheap mat spread wide can't get through the gate, so they would need to break the gate, which is worth far more than the mat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mat is worth little, but bringing it in would ruin the expensive gate. The final line ties the demonstration back to their exact words, closing the riddle.
steps.whatToRemember: All through this passage, רבי יהושע beats the elders of אתונא by turning their own tricks back on them, and in the last riddle he wins by showing them a real example.

phrases.english: Bring, each and every one, a mat, and spread it out.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets. Either way, each elder brings his own mat.

phrases.english: It would not go in through the gate.
He said to them: Bring axes and break it down.
phrases.notes: 'It' means the gate, which they would have to break so the wide mat could get through.

phrases.english: This is a utensil that is not worth the damage it causes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the demand in step 58 with a live demonstration.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A cheap mat that forces you to break an expensive gate.

steps.title: Each elder is brought aboard and fooled by the sixty mattresses
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע brings each elder onto his ship. Each one sees sixty mattresses and assumes all his colleagues are coming to that room.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought each and every one of them. When each one saw sixty mattresses, he said: All my colleagues are coming here.
steps.whatsHappening: The contest is over, so the story moves on. רבי יהושע brings the elders onto his ship, and each one is tricked into staying in his room.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each elder sees sixty mattresses set out in his room. He concludes that his fellow elders will be joining him there. So he waits calmly and does not try to leave, even though he is actually alone.

phrases.english: He brought them, each and every one,
phrases.notes: He's bringing them onto his ship, as they agreed if he won. Each elder goes into his own separate room.

phrases.english: when he saw sixty mattresses,
phrases.notes: Each elder sees sixty mattresses in his own room, as if it were set up for the whole group.

phrases.english: he said: All my colleagues are coming here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the final riddle (the mat that broke the gate), the contest is over. The story moves to the prize: bringing the elders onto the ship.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each elder is brought aboard and stays put, thinking his colleagues will join him.

steps.title: רבי יהושע tells the sailor to set sail
steps.stepSummary: With the elders settled on board, רבי יהושע orders the sailor to release the ship and start sailing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to the sailor: Release your ship.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the elders are quietly on board, רבי יהושע gives the order to sail away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trick with the mattresses worked. No elder is trying to leave, so the ship can set off and carry them away from Athens.

phrases.english: He said to the sailor:
Release your ship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues directly: the elders are settled on board, so now the ship leaves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ship sets sail with the elders aboard.

steps.title: On the way, he takes out earth from their homeland
steps.stepSummary: While they are traveling, רבי יהושע takes some earth from the elders' own land. This sets up the next part of the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: While they were coming, he took some earth from their earth.
steps.whatsHappening: During the voyage, רבי יהושע takes out some earth from Athens. This is a setup line that prepares the next scene of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The text simply says he took earth from 'their earth,' meaning the soil of the elders' homeland. Why he does this is not explained yet. The story will use it in the next part.

keyTerms.meaning: While they were coming or traveling

phrases.english: While they were coming
he took dirt from their dirt.
phrases.notes: 'Their dirt' means the soil of their homeland, Athens. Hold onto this, because the story is about to use it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the voyage scene and sets up what comes next.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע takes earth from the elders' homeland during the journey.
